context.in_practice: With route 1, the "watching" message only appears once the program is actually listening for changes and has finished its first import or sync. Anything you change after you see it gets picked up. If you stop the program while it is still starting, the message never appears, so you won't see "watching" just before it exits. Route 2 doesn't consider when the message should appear. It prints wherever it already happened to print, which may be before the program is really listening. Users then can't rely on it as a "ready" signal, and a quick stop during startup may still print it.
context.stakes: Someone watching a folder for changes needs to know when it is safe to start editing. If the "watching" message shows up too early, edits made right after it can be silently missed. If it shows up while the program is already shutting down, it gives a false sense that watching is active.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 delays the message until after the first import or sync, so it can take noticeably longer to appear on a large folder. Route 2 costs nothing to build, but the message makes no promise that changes will be caught.

plan_why: The question is when `config watch` prints its `watching <dir>` line (after handlers and the initial import/reconcile are in place, and skipped if a stop arrives during start-up). The only command that prints it is `watch`, which the sandbox forbids because it runs until SIGINT/SIGTERM. Seeing the difference would also need a file edit or signal timed against that line, which a fixed list of commands run one after another cannot do. Every other command (get, show, set, history) behaves the same under both routes.
routes: After handlers are installed and the initial import or reconcile; skipped if a stop came during start
